executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior

# Dust

A small command-line tool to quickly see which directories and files are using the most disk space.

Demo:

![Example](media/snap.png)

Overview

Dust prints a compact view of the biggest subdirectories or files. It automatically recurses into large subtrees so you can quickly find the biggest consumers of disk space. The display uses bars and colors to indicate relative usage and which parent folders subfolders belong to.

Usage

```
Usage: dust
Usage: dust <dir>
Usage: dust <dir> <another_dir> <and_more>
Usage: dust -p  (full-path - Show fullpath of the subdirectories)
Usage: dust -s  (apparent-size - shows the length of the file as opposed to the amount of disk space it uses)
Usage: dust -n 30  (Shows 30 directories instead of the default [default is terminal height])
Usage: dust -d 3  (Shows 3 levels of subdirectories)
Usage: dust -D (Show only directories)
Usage: dust -F (Show only files - finds your largest files)
Usage: dust -r (reverse order of output)
Usage: dust -o si/b/kb/kib/mb/mib/gb/gib (output format)
Usage: dust -X ignore  (ignore all files and directories with the name 'ignore')
Usage: dust -x (Only show directories on the same filesystem)
Usage: dust -b (Do not show percentages or draw ASCII bars)
Usage: dust -B (--bars-on-right - Percent bars moved to right side of screen)
Usage: dust -i (Do not show hidden files)
Usage: dust -c (No colors [monochrome])
Usage: dust -C (Force colors)
Usage: dust -f (Count files instead of diskspace)
Usage: dust -t (Group by filetype)
Usage: dust -z 10M (min-size, Only include files larger than 10M)
Usage: dust -e regex (Only include files matching this regex)
Usage: dust -v regex (Exclude files matching this regex)
Usage: dust -L (dereference-links - Treat symlinks as directories)
Usage: dust -P (Disable the progress indicator)
Usage: dust -R (For screen readers. Removes bars/symbols. Adds new column: depth level.)
Usage: dust -S (Custom Stack size)
Usage: dust --skip-total (No total row will be displayed)
Usage: dust -j (Prints JSON representation of directories)
Usage: dust --files0-from=FILE (Read NUL-terminated file paths from FILE)
Usage: dust --files-from=FILE (Read newline-terminated file paths from FILE)
Usage: dust --collapse=node-modules (Keep node_modules collapsed in display)
```

Config

Dust can read configuration from `~/.config/dust/config.toml` or `~/.dust.toml` to set default options.

Alternatives

- NCDU
- dutree
- dua
- pdu
- dirstat-rs

const MTIME_HELP: &str = "+/-n matches files modified more/less than n days ago , and n matches files modified exactly n days ago, days are rounded down.That is +n => (\u{2212}\u{221e}, curr\u{2212}(n+1)), n => [curr\u{2212}(n+1), curr\u{2212}n), and -n => (\u{1d450}\u{1d462}\u{1d45f}\u{1d45f}\u{2212}\u{1d45b}, +\u{221e})";

pub fn build_cli() -> Command {
    Command::new("Dust")
        .about("Like du but more intuitive")
        .version("1.2.3")
        .arg(
            Arg::new("depth")
                .short('d')
                .long("depth")
                .value_name("DEPTH")
                .value_parser(value_parser!(usize))
                .help("Depth to show")
                .num_args(1),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("threads")
                .short('T')
                .long("threads")
                .value_name("THREADS")
                .value_parser(value_parser!(usize))
                .help("Number of threads to use")
                .num_args(1),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("config")
                .long("config")
                .value_name("FILE")
                .value_hint(clap::ValueHint::FilePath)
                .help("Specify a config file to use")
                .num_args(1),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("number_of_lines")
                .short('n')
                .long("number-of-lines")
                .value_name("NUMBER")
                .value_parser(value_parser!(usize))
                .help("Number of lines of output to show. (Default is terminal_height - 10)")
                .num_args(1),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("display_full_paths")
                .short('p')
                .long("full-paths")
                .action(ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .help("Subdirectories will not have their path shortened"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("ignore_directory")
                .short('X')
                .long("ignore-directory")
                .value_name("PATH")
                .value_hint(clap::ValueHint::AnyPath)
                .action(ArgAction::Append)
                .num_args(1)
                .help("Exclude any file or directory with this path"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("ignore_all_in_file")
                .short('I')
                .long("ignore-all-in-file")
                .value_name("FILE")
                .value_hint(clap::ValueHint::FilePath)
                .num_args(1)
                .help("Exclude any file or directory with a regex matching that listed in this file, the file entries will be added to the ignore regexs provided by --invert_filter"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("dereference_links")
                .short('L')
                .long("dereference-links")
                .action(ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .help("dereference sym links - Treat sym links as directories and go into them"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("limit_filesystem")
                .short('x')
                .long("limit-filesystem")
                .action(ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .help("Only count the files and directories on the same filesystem as the supplied directory"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("display_apparent_size")
                .short('s')
                .long("apparent-size")
                .action(ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .help("Use file length instead of blocks"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("reverse")
                .short('r')
                .long("reverse")
                .action(ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .help("Print tree upside down (biggest highest)"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("no_colors")
                .short('c')
                .long("no-colors")
                .action(ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .help("No colors will be printed (Useful for commands like: watch)"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("force_colors")
                .short('C')
                .long("force-colors")
                .action(ArgAction::SetTrue)
                .help("Force colors print"),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("no_bars")
                .short('b')

                .help("No percent bars or percentages will be displayed"),

        .arg(
            Arg::new("min_size")

// Runtime helpers used by main: terminal detection, input lists, errors.
use std::io::{BufRead, Read};
use std::path::PathBuf;

use regex::Regex;

use crate::dir_walker::RuntimeErrors;

pub const DEFAULT_NUMBER_OF_LINES: usize = 30;
pub const DEFAULT_TERMINAL_WIDTH: usize = 80;
pub const DEFAULT_STACK_SIZE: usize = 64 * 1024 * 1024;
pub const MIN_STACK_SIZE: usize = 1024 * 1024;

pub fn terminal_size_of(fd: libc::c_int) -> Option<(usize, usize)> {
    unsafe {
        if libc::isatty(fd) != 1 {
            return None;
        }
        let mut ws: libc::winsize = std::mem::zeroed();
        if libc::ioctl(fd, libc::TIOCGWINSZ, &mut ws) == -1 {
            return None;
        }
        if ws.ws_col > 0 && ws.ws_row > 0 {
            Some((ws.ws_col as usize, ws.ws_row as usize))
        } else {
            None
        }
    }
}

pub fn get_terminal_size() -> Option<(usize, usize)> {
    terminal_size_of(libc::STDOUT_FILENO)
        .or_else(|| terminal_size_of(libc::STDERR_FILENO))
        .or_else(|| terminal_size_of(libc::STDIN_FILENO))
}

pub fn init_color(no_color: bool) -> bool {
    no_color
}

        .collect::<Vec<Regex>>();

    let by_filecount = options.get_flag("by_filecount");

/// Compile every regex given on the command line.
/// An invalid expression is fatal.
fn get_regex_value<'a, I: Iterator<Item = &'a String>>(maybe_value: Option<I>) -> Vec<Regex> {
    let values: Vec<&String> = match maybe_value {
        Some(v) => v.collect(),
        None => vec![],
    };
    values
        .into_iter()
        .map(|reg| {
            Regex::new(reg).unwrap_or_else(|err| {
                eprintln!("Ignoring bad value for regex {err:?}");
                std::process::exit(1)
            })
        })
        .collect()
}

/// Read the whole of stdin; unreadable or non UTF-8 input counts as empty.
fn read_all_stdin() -> String {
    let mut s = String::new();
    if std::io::stdin().lock().read_to_string(&mut s).is_err() {
        s.clear();
    }
    s
}

/// Split a list of paths separated by NUL bytes or by newlines.
/// Empty entries are skipped for NUL separated lists only.
fn split_paths(contents: &str, null_terminated: bool) -> Vec<PathBuf> {
    if null_terminated {
        contents
            .split('\0')
            .filter(|p| !p.is_empty())
            .map(PathBuf::from)
            .collect()
    } else {
        contents.lines().map(PathBuf::from).collect()
    }
}

/// Load the target list for --files-from / --files0-from.
///
/// `-` means stdin. When stdin provides nothing we fall back to the
/// current directory. A file which cannot be read also falls back to the
/// current directory, while an empty file yields an empty list.
fn read_paths_from_source(source: &str, null_terminated: bool) -> Vec<PathBuf> {
    let default_dir = || vec![PathBuf::from(".")];
    if source == "-" {
        let paths = split_paths(&read_all_stdin(), null_terminated);

/// Summarise the problems met during the walk on stderr.
///
/// Missing files are always listed, permission problems only when
/// --print-errors is given.
fn print_any_errors(print_errors: bool, errors: &RuntimeErrors) {
    if !errors.file_not_found.is_empty() {
        let err = errors.file_not_found.join(", ");
        eprintln!("No such file or directory: {err}");
    }
    if !errors.no_permissions.is_empty() {
        if print_errors {
            let err = errors.no_permissions.join(", ");
            eprintln!("Did not have permissions for directories: {err}");
        } else {
            eprintln!(
                "Did not have permissions for all directories (add --print-errors to see errors)"
            );
        }
    }
    if !errors.unknown_error.is_empty() {
        let err = errors.unknown_error.join(", ");
        eprintln!("Unknown Error: {err}");
    }
}

I've rebuilt the tool from scratch in Rust: it's Dust 1.2.3, a `du`-like disk usage viewer. Across several thousand comparison runs it matched the original's stdout, stderr and exit code, except in a few cases where the original's own output changes from run to run (listed below). Everything is committed. `compile.sh` builds from the local crate cache without network access, and I checked it on a fresh clone; the result was byte-identical to my development build.

**How I tested it.** I wrote scripts that run both binaries on the same input and compare the three outputs. They covered:
- about 30 test directories, including hard links, symlinks and loops, broken links, special files, unreadable directories, unicode and invalid UTF-8 names, sparse files and very deep trees;
- every option and many combinations, including random fuzzing of flags, colour settings and invalid command lines;
- config files, `--files-from` / `--files0-from` from files and stdin, and the time filters under several `TZ` values;
- real terminals (via tmux and a pseudo-terminal), terminal widths 1–100, and large trees such as `/usr` and `/`, where speed matched the original.

**Behaviours I copied that you might not expect:**
- Colours are used when any of stdout, stderr or stdin is a terminal, not just stdout. They are also turned off if `NO_COLOR` is set to any value, even an empty one.
- Day boundaries for `-M`/`-A`/`-y` are local midnight. A `TZ` value with a daylight-saving name but no rules (e.g. `EST5EDT`) is treated as UTC, as the original does when no zoneinfo file exists.
- The open-file limit is raised at startup, so very deep trees don't fail.
- Crash messages report the same source file, line and column as the original's. The thread number inside those messages varies on every run, so it can never match exactly.

**Where results can still differ, because the original is random:**
- When targets overlap without one containing the other (e.g. `dust . a`), the original picks which copy of the shared files to count at random. Mine always uses the command-line order.
- With several missing paths, the original lists them in a random order in "No such file or directory: …". Mine keeps command-line order.
- The progress spinner depends on timing. After a startup crash (e.g. a bad `-M` value), whether a trailing clear-line sequence appears is a race in both.

**Known gaps:**
- My default thread stack is 64 MB; the original uses 1 GB when memory allows, which only matters for extremely deep trees.
- I raise very small `-S` values to 1 MB, so mine may survive where the original would overflow its stack.
- The original reports permission errors under `/proc/self/ns` that mine doesn't. That comes from the original binary not being readable, not from a logic difference.

The code is in `src/`, organised as command line, config, walker, selection, file-type grouping, drawing, colours and progress.

The reimplementation is finished and committed. A fresh clone builds with `./compile.sh` and produces `./executable`, which matches the original's output on every reproducible test I ran.

**How I tested it:** I ran the original and my build side by side on the same inputs and compared stdout, stderr and exit codes byte for byte. That covered:
- every command-line flag, conflict and error message (about 1,000 random argument combinations)
- around 1,500 random flag combinations over about 40 test directories, including hard links, symlinks and loops, unreadable folders, odd and unicode file names, sparse files and very deep trees
- every terminal width from 1 to 90, real terminal sessions, config files, `LS_COLORS`/`NO_COLOR`, time zones, and file lists read from stdin or files
- performance, which is the same as the original on `/usr` and `/`

**Where the two can still differ:** these all vary from run to run in the original too, so exact matching isn't possible.
- When several missing paths are reported, the original lists them in random order; mine uses the order given.
- When two targets overlap without one containing the other (e.g. `dust . a`), which one keeps the shared files depends on the original's random internal ordering.
- The progress spinner, and whether a final `\r \r` appears after a crash, depend on timing.
- Crash messages contain an OS thread id that changes every run. I placed the code so the file and line numbers in those messages match the original's.

**Choices you might want to know about:**
- **Rust and crates:** it's written in Rust using crates from the machine's local cache (clap, regex, serde, toml, rayon and a few others). `compile.sh` builds offline and only goes to the network if those crates are missing. Using the same argument-parsing library as the original keeps its help and error text identical.
- **Stack size:** the default worker-thread stack is 64 MB. The original appears to use 1 GB when memory allows. This only matters for extremely deep folder trees.
- **`compile.sh` deletes `./executable` first.** In this workspace that means it replaces the original binary.
- **`/proc/self`:** the original reports permission errors there and mine doesn't. That comes from the original binary file being unreadable, not from any difference in my code.

`.gitignore` excludes `target/` and `executable`.
